body.en: This chapter covers the applied mathematical structures exclusive to Applications and Interpretation HL: matrix algebra, Markov chain stochastic modeling, graph algorithms (Kruskal, Prim, Dijkstra), eigenvalue diagonalization, and coupled differential equation phase plane topology.

label.en: ● Level 1 Foundation — Matrix Algebra & Graph Topology

body.en:
Matrix Operations & Inversion: For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\):

\[ \det A = ad - bc. \quad \text{If } \det A \neq 0, \quad A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc} \begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}. \]

To solve the linear system \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\), premultiply by \(A^{-1}\): \[ \mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}. \]

Graph Theory (Networks) Fundamentals:

  • A graph \(G = (V, E)\) consists of a non-empty set of vertices \(V\) and a set of edges \(E\). The degree \(\deg(v)\) is the number of edges incident to \(v\).
  • Euler's Handshaking Lemma: The sum of the degrees of all vertices equals twice the number of edges: \[ \sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|. \] Consequently, the number of vertices with odd degree is always even.
  • Adjacency Matrix \(A\): A matrix where entry \(a_{ij}\) represents the number of edges between vertex \(i\) and vertex \(j\). The entry \((A^k)_{ij}\) in the \(k\)-th matrix power gives the exact number of walks of length \(k\) from vertex \(i\) to vertex \(j\).
  • Eulerian Circuits & Trails: An Eulerian trail (visits every edge once) exists \(\iff\) exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree. An Eulerian circuit (closed loop) exists \(\iff\) all vertices have even degree.
  • Hamiltonian Cycles: A closed loop visiting every vertex exactly once.

label.en: ▲ Level 2 Analytical Tools — Markov Chains, Steady States & MST Algorithms

body.en:
Markov Chains & Transition Matrices: A Markov chain is a discrete-time stochastic process with state space \(\{S_1, S_2, \dots, S_m\}\). In the IB AI HL convention, the transition matrix \(T\) is column-stochastic:

\[ T_{ij} = P(\text{State } i \text{ at step } n+1 \mid \text{State } j \text{ at step } n), \quad \sum_{i=1}^m T_{ij} = 1. \]

The probability distribution vector \(\mathbf{p}_n\) evolves according to: \[ \mathbf{p}_{n+1} = T \mathbf{p}_n \implies \mathbf{p}_n = T^n \mathbf{p}_0. \] Steady-State Distribution Vector \(\mathbf{s}\): A probability vector satisfying \(T\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{s}\) with \(\sum s_i = 1\). Thus \(\mathbf{s}\) is an eigenvector of \(T\) corresponding to eigenvalue \(\lambda = 1\), found by solving \((T - I)\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{0}\).

Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) & Shortest Path Algorithms: For a connected weighted graph on \(V\) vertices, a spanning tree connects all \(V\) vertices using exactly \(V - 1\) edges with minimum total edge weight:

  • Kruskal's Algorithm: Sort all edges in non-decreasing order of weight. Greedily add the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle, stopping when \(V - 1\) edges are selected.
  • Prim's Algorithm: Start at any arbitrary vertex. At each step, add the minimum-weight edge connecting a vertex in the growing tree to a vertex not yet in the tree.
  • Dijkstra's Algorithm: Determines the shortest path from a starting source vertex to all other vertices using permanent and temporary distance labels.

note.en: The transition matrix is T = [[P(A→A), 1−P(B→B)], [1−P(A→A), P(B→B)]]. For a regular chain (not both P(A→A) and P(B→B) at the same extreme), whatever starting P(A) you choose, the curve settles onto the dashed steady-state line πA = (1−P(B→B)) / [(1−P(A→A))+(1−P(B→B))] — an eigenvector of T for eigenvalue 1, exactly as defined above. Try starting P(A) = 0 vs 1 with the same P(A→A), P(B→B): different paths, same destination. Push both sliders to the same edge and that regularity breaks: at P(A→A) = P(B→B) = 1 every state is absorbing, so the chain never moves at all and 'steady state' is just wherever you started; at P(A→A) = P(B→B) = 0 the chain swaps states every single step and never settles — it oscillates between P(A) and 1−P(A) forever.

label.en: ▲ Level 3 University Rigor — Theorem: Eigen-Decomposition & Coupled Linear Systems

body.en:
Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors: A scalar \(\lambda \in \mathbb{C}\) and non-zero vector \(\mathbf{v}\) satisfy \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) if and only if: \[ \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 \quad (\text{the characteristic equation}). \] For each eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\), the corresponding eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}_i\) spans the nullspace \(\ker(A - \lambda_i I)\).

Matrix Diagonalization: If \(A\) possesses \(n\) linearly independent eigenvectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n\), then: \[ A = PDP^{-1}, \quad \text{where } P = [\mathbf{v}_1 \; \dots \; \mathbf{v}_n], \quad D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n). \] Matrix powers are evaluated directly in diagonal coordinates: \[ A^k = P D^k P^{-1} = P \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1^k & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2^k \end{pmatrix} P^{-1}. \]

Coupled Systems of Differential Equations: Consider the linear system: \[ \frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = A\mathbf{x}, \quad \mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{pmatrix}. \] If \(A\) has distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\) with eigenvectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\), the general solution is: \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1 e^{\lambda_1 t}\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 e^{\lambda_2 t}\mathbf{v}_2. \] Phase Plane Topological Classification:

  • \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2 < 0\): Stable Node (Sink) — all trajectories approach the origin as \(t \to \infty\).
  • \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2 > 0\): Unstable Node (Source) — trajectories diverge away from origin.
  • \(\lambda_1 < 0 < \lambda_2\): Saddle Point (Unstable) — trajectories approach along \(\mathbf{v}_1\) and escape along \(\mathbf{v}_2\).
  • \(\lambda = \alpha \pm i\beta\): Spiral / Focus — trajectories spiral inward if \(\alpha < 0\), outward if \(\alpha > 0\), and form closed elliptical orbits (Center) if \(\alpha = 0\).

label.en: Worked Example AI.1 — Matrix Inversion & System Solving

problem.en: Solve the linear system using matrix inversion: \[ 2x + 3y = 7, \qquad x - y = 1. \]

solution.en:
1. Formulate in matrix vector form \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] 2. Calculate the determinant: \[ \det A = 2(-1) - 3(1) = -2 - 3 = -5 \neq 0. \] 3. Find the inverse matrix \(A^{-1}\): \[ A^{-1} = \frac{1}{-5} \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.2 & 0.6 \\ 0.2 & -0.4 \end{pmatrix}. \] 4. Multiply \(\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.2 & 0.6 \\ 0.2 & -0.4 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.2(7) + 0.6(1) \\ 0.2(7) - 0.4(1) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.4 + 0.6 \\ 1.4 - 0.4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Solution: \(x = 2, \; y = 1\).

label.en: Worked Example AI.2 — Markov Chain Steady-State Vector

problem.en: A market contains two competing internet providers, A and B. Each year, 80% of customers with A remain with A, while 20% switch to B. For provider B, 70% remain with B while 30% switch to A. (a) Write down the transition matrix \(T\). (b) Determine the long-term steady-state market share for both providers.

solution.en:
(a) Transition matrix \(T\):
Column 1 represents transitions from A: \[ P(A\to A) = 0.8, \quad P(B\to A) = 0.2. \] Column 2 represents transitions from B: \[ P(A\to B) = 0.3, \quad P(B\to B) = 0.7. \] Thus the column-stochastic transition matrix is: \[ T = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}. \]

(b) Long-term steady state \(\mathbf{s} = \begin{pmatrix} s_A \\ s_B \end{pmatrix}\):
Solve \(T\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{s}\) subject to \(s_A + s_B = 1\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} s_A \\ s_B \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} s_A \\ s_B \end{pmatrix} \implies 0.8 s_A + 0.3 s_B = s_A \implies -0.2 s_A + 0.3 s_B = 0. \] Thus: \[ 0.2 s_A = 0.3 s_B \implies s_A = 1.5 s_B. \] Substitute into the probability normalization constraint \(s_A + s_B = 1\): \[ 1.5 s_B + s_B = 1 \implies 2.5 s_B = 1 \implies s_B = \frac{1}{2.5} = 0.40. \] Then \(s_A = 1 - 0.40 = 0.60\).

Conclusion: In the steady state, Provider A holds 60% of the market and Provider B holds 40%.

problem.en: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\). Hence find an expression for \(A^n\).

solution.en:
1. Characteristic equation \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\): \[ \det\begin{pmatrix} 4-\lambda & 1 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{pmatrix} = (4-\lambda)(3-\lambda) - 2 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 12 - 2 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = 0. \] Factor: \((\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2) = 0 \implies \lambda_1 = 5, \; \lambda_2 = 2\).

2. Eigenvector for \(\lambda_1 = 5\): \[ (A - 5I)\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \implies -x + y = 0 \implies y = x. \quad \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] 3. Eigenvector for \(\lambda_2 = 2\): \[ (A - 2I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \implies 2x + y = 0 \implies y = -2x. \quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}. \]

4. Form \(P\) and \(D\): \[ P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det P = -2 - 1 = -3, \quad P^{-1} = -\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. \] 5. Calculate \(A^n = P D^n P^{-1}\): \[ A^n = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 5^n & 0 \\ 0 & 2^n \end{pmatrix} \left[ \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \right] = \frac{1}{3} \begin{pmatrix} 2\cdot 5^n + 2^n & 5^n - 2^n \\ 2\cdot 5^n - 2\cdot 2^n & 5^n + 2\cdot 2^n \end{pmatrix}. \]

\( \sum \deg(v) = 2|E| \); odd degree vertex count is always even
A tree on \( V \) vertices always contains exactly \( V - 1 \) edges

label.en: ⚠ Topic AI HL Exam Traps: Transition Matrices & Graph Algorithms

body.en:
Column-Stochastic vs Row-Stochastic: The IB AI HL syllabus uses column-stochastic transition matrices where each column sums to 1: entry \(T_{ij}\) represents the probability of moving from state \(j\) to state \(i\). Multiplying \(T \mathbf{p}_n = \mathbf{p}_{n+1}\) requires a column vector. If you set up rows summing to 1 by mistake, standard matrix multiplications produce wrong states.

Cycle Detection in Kruskal's: In Kruskal's algorithm, check for cycles across the entire connected subgraph, not just whether both vertices have been visited. If two visited vertices already belong to the same component, connecting them creates a cycle and the edge must be rejected.

Eulerian Graph Conditions: An Eulerian trail (open path visiting every edge once) requires exactly two vertices of odd degree. An Eulerian circuit (closed loop returning to the start) requires all vertices to have even degree.

question.en: A weighted network has edges: DE = 1, BC = 2, AB = 3, CD = 4, BD = 5, CE = 6, AC = 7, AD = 8. Use Kruskal's algorithm to determine the minimum spanning tree and compute its total weight.

solution.en:
1. Sort all edges in non-decreasing order of weight:
DE (1), BC (2), AB (3), CD (4), BD (5), CE (6), AC (7), AD (8).
2. Select edges avoiding cycles:
- Add DE (weight 1) [Vertices connected: {D, E}]
- Add BC (weight 2) [Vertices connected: {D, E}, {B, C}]
- Add AB (weight 3) [Vertices connected: {D, E}, {A, B, C}]
- Add CD (weight 4) [Merges components: {A, B, C, D, E} - all 5 vertices connected!]
3. Check edge count: \(V - 1 = 5 - 1 = 4\) edges selected.
4. Total MST Weight: \[ 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. \]

question.en: A network has weighted adjacency matrix \(W\). Explain how the minimum spanning tree algorithm (Kruskal's) differs from Dijkstra's algorithm.

solution.en: Kruskal's algorithm finds a global minimum spanning tree that connects all vertices in the graph with minimum total edge weight, without reference to any single starting vertex. Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path routes from a designated single source vertex to all other individual vertices. A minimum spanning tree does not necessarily contain the shortest paths between arbitrary pairs of vertices.
